Should this piece explain the event or communicate our general values?
I keep changing the layout without making the message clearer.
How do I make the product distinction matter more than a generic slogan?
How can I focus a message without hiding important conditions?

related_patterns.relationship: Makes a chosen priority visible through relative size.
Establishes whose knowledge, task and viewing conditions matter.
Resolves a local ambiguity within the intended message.
Orders the supporting material around the intended takeaway.

visual_decision.reason: Three finished photographic design pairs change only two headline text nodes, separating the choice of message from scale, color or layout.

sources.supports: Distinguishing the main message from a call to action in public communication.
Beginning with evidence about audience needs rather than justifying existing content.

patterns.title: Design for the Audience
patterns.short_description: Adapt language, information priority, and presentation to people's knowledge, tasks, and viewing conditions.
use_when: The design assumes vocabulary its intended viewers have not learned.
Correct information is difficult to use in its actual viewing setting.
Organizational features lead while a visitor's decision details are secondary.
Stakeholders describe an audience by stereotypes rather than relevant tasks and knowledge.
goals: Make an encounter understandable for its intended viewers.
Prioritize information according to the task being performed.
Connect presentation choices to evidence about viewing conditions.
prerequisites: An initial audience and situation hypothesis, with research needed to verify it.
not_ideal_when: Audience assumptions are being treated as established research.
Several conflicting tasks require distinct routes or artifacts.
example_user_queries: Our poster uses terms that newcomers do not understand.
How can I design for an audience without stereotyping them?
People cannot find the directions on our entrance sign.
The information is correct but difficult to use in a busy setting.
Our booking page describes the building before explaining the day pass.
How do I decide what information this audience needs first?
Should expert terminology be explained or removed?
We are designing for several audiences with different needs.
How do viewing conditions change my design choices?
How can I test whether my assumptions about readers are correct?

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses what a specific piece should establish for its audience.
Makes a chosen audience-relevant priority visible through size.
Chooses the structure and format that support the resulting communication job.
Clarifies implications whose explanation depends on audience understanding.

visual_decision.reason: Three controlled photographic transformations demonstrate knowledge, setting and task mismatches. Four text nodes change in the pottery example; four text nodes plus sizes and baselines change in the sign; five fact text nodes change in the booking page. Unrelated variables remain fixed.

sources.supports: Research likely users, tasks, context and needs; treat unverified assumptions as hypotheses.
Varied abilities and situational barriers; transfer from web to print is explicitly editorial inference.

patterns.title: Match Form to Purpose
patterns.short_description: Choose a structure and format that let people use the information for the task the design must support.
use_when: An explanation is being used as a working procedure.
People must reconstruct comparisons from separate descriptions.
A fixed display needs to offer portable details.
The format was chosen before the communication job was established.
goals: Choose a structure that supports the intended encounter.
Keep necessary facts while changing how people can use them.
Judge the artifact in use rather than by style preference.
prerequisites: An audience, communication objective and reliable underlying material.
not_ideal_when: The purpose is unresolved or the information is false.
An arbitrary numbered sequence or comparison grid would distort the content.
example_user_queries: The information is correct but people cannot use it while working.
Should this be a paragraph, numbered instructions or a checklist?
People have to read several descriptions to compare our options.
We chose a poster but people need details they can take away.
Our template looks good but does not suit the job.
How can I choose the right format for this information?
The design needs to explain a process and support doing it.
Would a comparison table help or oversimplify the options?
Our display attracts attention but provides no useful takeaway.
How do I balance expressive presentation with practical use?

related_patterns.relationship: Establishes whose knowledge, tasks and viewing conditions matter.
Determines the takeaway the chosen form must communicate.
Arranges progression within the chosen artifact or structure.

visual_decision.reason: Three controlled transformations isolate the functional body region: paragraph to procedure, descriptions to comparison table, single address to cuttable tabs. Shared photography and fixed content remain identical.

sources.supports: Use rows and columns to support comparison; accessible table captions and headers in digital use.
Distinguish ordered action journeys from reading and alternatives; transfer to printed procedure is editorial inference.

patterns.title: Remove the Nonessential
patterns.short_description: Remove elements that do not earn their place in this encounter while preserving meaning, identity, and necessary conditions.
use_when: A prominent message is repeated without a separate communication role.
Decorative treatments accumulate without supporting information or identity.
Available metrics are included despite belonging to a different review.
A sparse visual style is being mistaken for useful editing.
goals: Remove weak contributions while retaining necessary meaning and conditions.
Judge inclusion against audience and purpose.
Distinguish deletion from changing prominence or hiding information.
prerequisites: An audience, communication purpose and a reliable account of what each element contributes.
not_ideal_when: Elements have an established recognition, emotional or independent-use role.
The problem concerns missing explanation or poor organization rather than expendable material.
example_user_queries: My design keeps accumulating badges and callouts.
How do I decide what can be removed without losing important information?
Our poster repeats the same offer in several places.
The label has several ornamental styles competing with the product name.
Our report contains metrics that do not answer its question.
I want a cleaner design but do not want to erase its character.
Should this detail be removed or just made less prominent?
How can I simplify a design without hiding its conditions?
When is repetition useful rather than unnecessary?
Does a dense design always need less content?

related_patterns.relationship: Establishes the takeaway against which contributions can be judged.
Determines which explanations and details matter to the intended viewer.
Changes prominence when an element should remain rather than be deleted.
Allocates purposeful open areas around retained elements; space need not be filled or created by deleting useful content.

visual_decision.reason: Three deletion-only photographic transformations remove a repeated badge, a seal and frame, or an off-task reporting block. Every retained element stays identical, with no reflow.

sources.supports: Practitioner guidance distinguishes relevance to user tasks from a minimalist visual trend and preserves necessary information.
Selected embellished charts preserved interpretation accuracy and improved delayed recall, a bounded counterexample to blanket minimalism.

patterns.title: Make Meaning Explicit
patterns.short_description: State the relationship, scope, or consequence that a viewer would otherwise have to infer from an ambiguous design.
use_when: An action is visible but its immediate result is unclear.
A precise figure lacks a definition or denominator.
A product photograph leaves the price scope ambiguous.
The designer knows a relationship that the viewer must infer.
goals: Resolve consequential ambiguity at the point of use.
State only meanings supported by the actual offer, workflow or evidence.
Keep clarification concise and near the element it explains.
prerequisites: An accurate account of what the action, measure or offer actually means.
not_ideal_when: The underlying behavior or evidence is unknown.
Ambiguity intentionally supports an expressive purpose.
A familiar convention is already dependable in context and further explanation adds noise.
example_user_queries: People can find the button but do not know what it will do.
Does this action send a request or confirm a booking?
Our percentage looks precise but nobody knows what it counts.
How can I explain the denominator without cluttering the report?
Customers cannot tell which items the price includes.
The product photo makes an accessory look included.
The designer understands this label but new readers interpret it differently.
How much explanation does this interface need?
Our important qualification is far from the claim it explains.
How do I make uncertainty clear without making an unsupported promise?

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses the takeaway of the whole piece rather than resolving one local ambiguity.
Establishes which assumptions the intended viewer can reasonably bring.
Preserves clarifications that earn their place even when their deletion would look cleaner.
Addresses the specific ambiguity created when a meaningful distinction relies only on color.

visual_decision.reason: Three text-only transformations specify an action consequence, a measure and denominator, and a product-price scope. All unrelated elements remain identical.

sources.supports: Name a button according to the action it performs; Continue remains appropriate for some progression steps.
Provide concise chart text identifying the measure and contextual coverage. Application to a numeric callout is editorial inference.

patterns.title: Chunk Information
patterns.short_description: Organize material into useful units so readers can locate a part, understand what belongs together, and handle detail without reconstructing the structure.
use_when: A complete list lacks useful entry points for recurring questions.
Facts about each record are scattered among field-based groups.
A reference must be read aloud or checked in manageable segments.
goals: Choose content units that match the actual task.
Preserve necessary facts and their relationships.
Express grouping without implying an untested memory benefit.
prerequisites: Accurate content and a known reading or checking task.
not_ideal_when: Continuous prose or a short list already suits the reading task.
A comparison table better supports cross-record scanning.
Inserted separators would alter an identifier accepted by the receiving system.
example_user_queries: All the information is here but readers cannot find the right part.
How should I group the practical details on an invitation?
Our booking summary makes people match three separate lists.
Should these cards group by field or by booking?
The reference number is hard to read aloud.
How do I divide information without deleting important facts?
Does every information group need a box?
How can I stop a page from becoming too many tiny cards?
Should I apply the seven-item rule to this layout?
How do I keep a qualification with the detail it limits?

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses the artifact or structure for a job; chunking chooses the units within it.
Clarifies labels and relationships; the grouped facts must still form a coherent unit.
Orders the useful units that chunking defines.
Makes useful content units perceptible through relative distance; it does not decide their semantic boundaries.

visual_decision.reason: Three controlled transformations add question-based headings, regroup unchanged booking values into records, and insert two reference separators. Unrelated imagery, styling and presentation remain fixed.

sources.supports: Headings communicate organization and support navigation when correctly implemented. Application to print is editorial inference.
Memory chunks depend on prior associations and task conditions; this review does not prescribe group counts for these layouts.

patterns.title: Sequence the Message
patterns.short_description: Arrange content so readers encounter context, dependencies, and supporting detail in an order suited to what they need to understand or do.
use_when: A request precedes the context needed to judge it.
A reference order obscures the dependencies of a first-time task.
An analytical process order delays the finding a short review exists to communicate.
goals: Choose a progression suited to the encounter.
Put necessary context before its use.
Keep qualifications with claims and preserve meaningful order in alternative presentations.
prerequisites: Accurate content and an understanding of the actual task or process.
not_ideal_when: Independent items are meant for lookup or comparison.
A familiar action needs a direct route without repeated explanation.
An intentional narrative or exploratory experience calls for another progression.
example_user_queries: Our page asks people to book before it explains the event.
The information is complete but people keep going back to earlier sections.
Which detail should come before the action?
Our guide is alphabetical but new customers need to follow the process.
The instructions explain the prerequisite too late.
Should a short report start with its method or its finding?
How do I lead with the result without hiding its limitations?
Do these topics actually need a fixed order?
Returning visitors have to read the same introduction again.
The visual arrangement and screen reader order tell different stories.

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses coherent units; sequencing arranges their progression.
Chooses the artifact or structure within which a progression is appropriate.
Defines what the piece should establish; sequencing prepares, develops and qualifies it.
Makes the chosen progression visually apparent and preserves it across presentations.

visual_decision.reason: Three order-only comparisons move intact content units: context before a request, prerequisites before dependent steps, and a finding before method. Unrelated imagery and typography remain fixed.

sources.supports: Write procedures in task order and provide preparation ahead of the task.
Frontload important online content; application to the fictional print review is editorial inference.
Preserve a programmatically determinable meaningful reading sequence; independent content may admit multiple valid orders.

patterns.title: Establish a Focal Point
patterns.short_description: Give a meaningful element or group a distinct leading role so the composition offers a useful place to begin.
use_when: Several elements share the strongest treatment despite an intended lead.
A pricing or other practical unit needs a local visual anchor.
Repeated primary treatments leave an action group without a leading role.
goals: Choose a content-bearing anchor suited to the encounter.
Distinguish the anchor without removing access to supporting detail.
Evaluate local focus and competing emphasis rather than assuming a guaranteed first fixation.
mechanisms: spatial isolation of an intact group
prerequisites: A clear communication purpose and a reason for the chosen element to lead.
not_ideal_when: Equal-status information should remain comparable.
Exploratory or reference use benefits from distributed attention.
The proposed anchor is irrelevant or misleading for the actual task.
example_user_queries: Everything on the poster seems equally important.
Where should someone start looking at this layout?
The event title competes with all its supporting attractions.
Can I give something emphasis without making it bigger?
The price is readable but it gets lost in the specification list.
How can white space help a practical detail stand out?
Every button looks like the main action.
Can I make the main action clearer by quieting the others?
Does every design need one dominant element?
My decorative badge gets more attention than the message.
How do I keep qualifications attached to a prominent price?

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses what a piece should establish; a focal point gives a meaningful part of that intention a visible leading role.
Supplies one means of prominence; focal points can also use weight, isolation or reduced competition.
Uses purposeful differences to establish an anchor, while contrast also distinguishes peer categories and roles.
Aligns cues around a focal point with useful destinations.

visual_decision.reason: Three controlled comparisons change only one headline weight, a pricing-group horizontal translation, or secondary-action paints. No font sizes change, and unrelated artwork and presentation remain fixed.

sources.supports: Relative emphasis and audience-dependent priority; applications through weight and isolation are editorial interpretation.
Multiple influences on attentional guidance; no guarantee of first fixation for these fictional layouts.
Distinguish main and secondary actions; avoid multiple default buttons. The custom outlined treatment is original.
Preserve meaning through visible cues beyond hue where color conveys information or prompts action.

patterns.title: Create Deliberate Contrast
patterns.short_description: Use a visible difference in a chosen attribute to clarify a meaningful distinction, while keeping unrelated elements consistent.
use_when: Practical text barely separates from its background.
Similar category treatments make matching or tracing difficult.
Different voices or roles need a consistent visual distinction.
goals: Give each visible difference a meaningful job.
Choose a suitable attribute rather than changing everything.
Preserve equal status where distinction does not imply hierarchy.
prerequisites: A defined distinction that matters to the reader.
not_ideal_when: Equal treatments correctly express equal roles.
Extra differences would create an unexplained visual code.
A different attribute conflicts with a stable convention or reproduction constraint.
example_user_queries: Our invitation looks tasteful but the practical text is too faint.
How do I make a difference visible without redesigning the whole page?
The two chart lines are hard to tell apart at crossings.
Do I need to make one data series more important to distinguish them?
People have to match two very similar colors in the legend.
Can line pattern identify a category as well as color?
The interviewer and speaker look like one continuous voice.
How can I distinguish type roles while keeping the sizes fixed?
There are lots of differences but none seem meaningful.
Does a high text contrast ratio mean the composition is good?
When should two elements keep the same visual treatment?

related_patterns.relationship: Selects a leading anchor; contrast can also distinguish equal-status categories and voices.
Uses the size channel specifically; the three new examples preserve all font sizes.
Concentrates on light-dark relationships as one channel of purposeful contrast.
Uses wording or form differences to carry the meaning otherwise encoded only by hue.

visual_decision.reason: Three controlled transformations change only four text fills, the Evening plot and legend dash pattern, or three response lines’ font family and style. No font size, content, unrelated position, image or presentation changes.

sources.supports: Relative visible distinctions; concrete pattern and typographic-role applications are editorial interpretation.
Text-background contrast ratios and their web accessibility scope; specified color measurements do not certify a print artifact.
Use additional visible cues where color conveys category information.

patterns.title: Differentiate Levels of Importance
patterns.short_description: Assign content to meaningful levels and give each role a consistent visual treatment, while keeping necessary detail accessible.
use_when: Distinct content roles have collapsed into one visual level.
Repeated records give equivalent roles inconsistent treatments.
A promotional line outranks a condition needed to judge an offer.
goals: Assign importance against the reader’s task.
Make equivalent roles visually dependable.
Preserve necessary details and qualifications while reducing competing emphasis.
prerequisites: Accurate content and a clear reading or decision task.
not_ideal_when: Equal-status choices or reference entries should remain comparable.
Proposed levels cannot be distinguished in the intended reproduction.
Reader priorities differ enough to need another structure or direct route.
example_user_queries: The title, deadline and host all look equally important.
How do I decide what belongs in the supporting level?
Our booking cards make the same kind of information look different.
The reference code is bold in one record but quiet in another.
The price is clear but the restrictions are almost invisible.
A slogan gets more emphasis than a condition that changes the offer.
How do I keep reference information readable without making it the headline?
Does every page need exactly three levels?
Which content should receive each recurring text style?
Our hierarchy keeps gaining new exceptions for every stakeholder.
Can I establish importance without changing any type sizes?

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses an anchor; importance levels organize supporting and repeated roles around it.
Provides one means of expression; only the first comparison uses size changes.
Creates visible differences, including between peers; levels assign ranked roles consistently.
Coordinates recurring size relationships to implement established ranks without deciding their meaning.

visual_decision.reason: A course notice changes only four font sizes to express three roles; repeated booking records change only second-card weights/tones; an offer promotes a material condition and quiets its slogan without moving or rewriting anything.

sources.supports: Relative importance and audience-dependent priorities; the concrete role maps are original editorial proposals.
Heading ranks organize semantic sections and subsections, rather than simply promotional importance.
Informational web text needs adequate text-background distinction even when styled as secondary.

patterns.title: Establish a Clear Reading Order
patterns.short_description: Make the intended route through content apparent through sequence cues, continuity, and layouts that preserve meaningful order across presentations.
use_when: An existing procedure looks like independent reference cards.
A story continuation sits beneath an unrelated aside.
A narrow layout contradicts its numbered or underlying source sequence.
goals: Make the intended start and succession recognizable.
Distinguish the main thread from independent material.
Preserve meaningful order in visual and programmatic representations.
prerequisites: A meaningful content sequence and known relationships between independent threads.
not_ideal_when: Browsing, lookup or comparison permits several equally useful routes.
Numbering would impose a false procedure on independent items.
The underlying message or instructions need correction before layout can express them.
example_user_queries: Where should the reader go after this paragraph?
Our procedure looks like four independent topics.
The closing paragraph seems to belong to the sidebar.
Can I clarify the route without adding lots of arrows?
The layout has a strong title but the continuation is ambiguous.
Our numbered steps appear as one, three, two on a phone.
Desktop looks right but the narrow layout changes the order.
The source list is correct but the visible positions contradict it.
How do I keep an optional aside from interrupting the story?
Does every page need one compulsory reading route?
How do I distinguish deciding the message order from displaying it clearly?

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses the meaningful progression; reading order makes it legible.
Assigns rank; equal-ranked units may still require a strict succession.
Chooses useful units; reading order governs movement between units and separation of parallel threads.
Supports directional connections beyond sequential text, including looking between a caption and image.

visual_decision.reason: One comparison adds numbers only, one moves an intact continuation sideways, and one exchanges two intact narrow-screen steps. A companion responsive prototype verifies source and visual order at desktop and phone widths.

sources.supports: Numbered steps express procedures; application to the printed seed sheet is editorial interpretation.
Preserve programmatically determinable order where meaning depends on it; independent content can permit multiple valid sequences.
Matching DOM and visual order is one technique for preserving sequential relationships, not the only conformance method.

patterns.title: Guide the Eye
patterns.short_description: Orient visual cues toward useful destinations so attention has a coherent invitation to continue.
use_when: A directional subject faces away from the content it introduces.
A caption and photographic detail need a clearer visual connection.
An arrow has no useful destination or contradicts the available action.
goals: Align directional suggestions with meaningful destinations.
Preserve useful alternatives to a compulsory linear route.
prerequisites: A useful connection between content regions and a known audience/task.
not_ideal_when: Independent choices deserve equivalent emphasis.
A cue would obscure the content or imply unavailable behavior.
The only explanation would depend on visual direction.
example_user_queries: The person in my poster seems to look off the page.
My photograph and invitation feel disconnected.
The caption names a detail but readers cannot easily find it.
Can an existing rule connect this caption to the photograph?
The arrow in my layout points into empty space.
My page suggests swiping but there is nothing to swipe.
How do I lead toward the booking action without enlarging everything?
Several arrows and diagonals seem to pull in different directions.
Does a diagram of an eye path prove readers will follow it?
When is an outward-facing portrait appropriate?

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses the anchor; directional cues can connect it to useful destinations.
Makes succession recognizable; directional guidance also supports two-way and nonsequential connections.
Chooses how ideas unfold before cues express their connections.
Makes meaningful differences visible; visible cues still need meaningful destinations.

visual_decision.reason: One fixed-frame portrait is reflected, one existing leader is extended to a photographed patch, and one arrow is rerouted to an unchanged booking button. All unrelated variables stay fixed.

sources.supports: Original schematic-face gaze-cue experiment supports a limited claim about target detection, not poster performance.
Original contour-integration experiments support alignment/continuity in path detection, not a measured editorial reading benefit.
Instructions must not rely solely on sensory characteristics such as orientation or location.

patterns.title: Align to Common Edges
patterns.short_description: Give related elements shared reference edges so their placement expresses a clear and dependable relationship.
use_when: Related blocks have several unmotivated near-alignments.
Comparable numeric amounts have drifting right edges.
A nested component follows its outer boundary instead of its useful content inset.
goals: Give related elements dependable spatial references.
Choose alignment according to content and task.
Preserve local relationships inside nested components.
prerequisites: Related content and a known reading or comparison task.
not_ideal_when: Offsets express a meaningful content distinction.
Independent regions need different local references.
Mechanical alignment would cause clipping or ignore visible form.
example_user_queries: My poster has several slightly different left margins.
Every paragraph is left aligned but the page still looks scattered.
The date and website seem disconnected from the headline.
Should amounts in this table be centered or aligned to the right?
How do I make these prices easier to compare without enlarging them?
My card text starts at the border but its image is inset.
Which edge should a caption or text block follow?
Does everything on a page need to share one left edge?
How is aligning elements different from establishing a whole grid?
The guides line up but punctuation still looks uneven.

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses meaningful units; alignment can reinforce their relationships.
Clarifies traversal; a shared edge can support continuity without making independent items sequential.
Defines reusable columns, gutters and allowed spans beyond a local shared edge.
Makes equivalent gaps and insets repeat reliably; shared reference lines do not automatically settle distances.

visual_decision.reason: A poster consolidates three left edges, a cost column changes from centered to right-aligned, and an intact card-copy group moves to its existing content inset. Fonts, values, vertical positions and photographic sources remain fixed.

sources.supports: Flush-left text supplies a constant line starting point; extension across separate blocks is editorial interpretation.
Alignment between elements and with an underlying grid as part of considered layout relationships.
Right-align columns of numbers used for comparison; proper table structure remains necessary.

patterns.title: Establish a Grid
patterns.short_description: Define reusable margins, tracks, gutters, and spans so layout decisions form a coherent system that can adapt to content and format.
use_when: Repeated modules are internally consistent but have no reusable placement system.
A rigid one-track rule fragments text despite unused neighboring tracks.
A column count persists into a width where it no longer accommodates the content.
goals: Coordinate recurring positions and dimensions.
Allow different content roles to use appropriate spans.
Adapt layout structure to available width without shrinking typography.
prerequisites: Representative content, its roles, and the intended format or viewing conditions.
not_ideal_when: A simple composition needs only one local alignment relationship.
A rigid matrix would obstruct meaningful variation.
The content needs editorial clarification before its spatial structure can be chosen.
example_user_queries: My cards look consistent individually but the whole page feels improvised.
Where should a fifth program item go?
How do I choose a useful number of columns?
Do all elements have to occupy one cell of the grid?
My paragraph has lots of short lines but there is empty space beside it.
Can the image span the page while the text uses smaller regions?
Our desktop column count makes the phone layout cramped.
How can I adapt a grid without making the type smaller?
What is the difference between aligning edges and establishing a grid?
Does every empty track need to be filled?

related_patterns.relationship: Establishes local references; a grid coordinates reusable regions and spans.
Chooses roles that may receive different spans; the grid does not decide importance.
Makes succession recognizable; an orderly matrix alone can still leave traversal ambiguous.
Makes equivalent gaps and insets repeat reliably; shared reference lines do not automatically settle distances.

visual_decision.reason: Three intact cards move onto shared tracks, one paragraph expands its span and rewraps, and a narrow two-column course grid becomes one column while preserving content and type sizes. A diagram exposes the track/span system; a separate HTML study verifies the responsive policy.

sources.supports: Grid structures, margins, divisions, gutters and contextual choice within an identifiable design system.
Containers, columns, gutters and responsive variants; its 12-column implementation is not presented as universal.
Preserving information and functionality through adaptation rather than protecting a fixed column count; no full conformance claim.

patterns.title: Balance Visual Weight
patterns.short_description: Distribute visual weight across a composition so its parts form an intentional whole while preserving meaningful emphasis.
use_when: Substantial regions accumulate on one side without serving the brief.
Equal-sized peer panels carry markedly different tonal weight.
A necessary compact identifier contributes too little against a larger image.
goals: Make the distribution of prominent regions intentional.
Preserve meaningful hierarchy while adjusting balance.
Use existing content rather than decorative filler as a counterweight.
prerequisites: A communication brief and representative content in its actual format.
not_ideal_when: Deliberate imbalance serves the intended tension or movement.
Equalizing visual prominence would obscure the intended lead.
A quieter annotation is appropriate to an image-led experience.
example_user_queries: My invitation feels like everything is piled on the left.
Can I use the existing photograph to make the page feel more composed?
The boxes are the same size but one side still feels much heavier.
How do I stop a dark panel dominating its peer?
Does a balanced page have to be symmetrical?
Can a small text group balance a larger pale photograph?
I want the title to lead without the rest of the composition feeling abandoned.
Should I add decoration just to fill the empty side?
The grid is tidy but the whole page still feels lopsided.
When would an intentionally unbalanced composition be appropriate?

related_patterns.relationship: Selects the meaningful anchor; balance concerns its relationship to the rest of the field.
Makes differences visible; those differences contribute to weight whose distribution balance considers.
Coordinates positions and dimensions without guaranteeing equal perceived weight.
Allocates purposeful open areas around retained elements; space need not be filled or created by deleting useful content.

visual_decision.reason: An unchanged photograph moves across the page, a peer panel and its foreground are retuned, and a compact identifier changes only in font weight. All other content, typography, crops and presentation remain fixed.

sources.supports: Educational definition of balance, including symmetrical, asymmetrical and radial arrangements.
Relative weight through tone, contrast, typography, imagery and placement; no numerical visual-weight equation.
Imaginary-axis diagnostic and asymmetrical balance as identifiable design guidance, not a study of these examples.

patterns.title: Use Negative Space
patterns.short_description: Allocate open areas around, between and within elements to clarify relationships and give important content room without weakening necessary connections.
use_when: An image crowds a message while unused room exists elsewhere.
Headings float ambiguously between adjacent sections.
Copy presses against a container boundary despite surplus room inside it.
goals: Give open areas a communication role.
Keep necessary information while reallocating space.
Preserve meaningful connections and legibility.
prerequisites: Representative content, a defined viewer task and the intended format.
not_ideal_when: More separation would detach related information.
A compact reference requires dense comparison.
A deliberately crowded expression serves the brief.
example_user_queries: My poster feels cramped even though there is plenty of empty space.
How can I give the title room without deleting content?
Which gaps should be bigger than the others?
The section headings look detached from their text.
How much space belongs inside a product card?
Can negative space be a dark color?
Does whitespace mean making every layout minimal?
How can I keep related information together while separating sections?
When is a dense design appropriate?
Will adding space force the text to become too small?

related_patterns.relationship: Decides what can leave; negative space allocates room around retained material.
Defines meaningful units whose boundaries space can express.
Provides reference lines without determining the intervals around them.
Considers whole-composition prominence rather than specifying local gaps or insets.

visual_decision.reason: Three position-only interventions reallocate room above a photograph, around section headings and inside a fixed card. No content or type styles change.

sources.supports: Whitespace expresses relationships; headings should connect more closely to the text they introduce.
Deliberate open areas communicate structure; reassess spacing across screen sizes.
Proximity grouping and the risk of separating task-relevant information too far.

patterns.title: Establish Consistent Spacing
patterns.short_description: Assign repeatable spacing rules to equivalent relationships so gaps and insets communicate structure reliably while allowing content to vary.
use_when: Peer entries acquire inconsistent intervals without a content reason.
Repeated cards drift in their local copy insets.
Equivalent headings have unrelated gaps before the following text.
goals: Give equivalent relationships repeatable distances.
Preserve meaningful distinctions between spacing roles.
Keep layout rules usable when content lengths vary.
prerequisites: Representative content, intended format and identified content roles.
not_ideal_when: Different intervals express genuine hierarchy or separate categories.
Literal fixed positions would cause variable-length content to collide.
Intentional expressive rhythm requires considered variation.
example_user_queries: The same kind of entry has a different gap every time.
My cards use the same type but still look like different templates.
How do I choose which distances should repeat?
Do all gaps need to be the same size?
The paragraph is too far from one heading and too close to another.
A two-line heading breaks my spacing.
How can I stop small layout differences accumulating across pages?
Do I need an eight-pixel grid for print design?
Should a longer card have the same starting positions?
When should spacing deliberately vary?

related_patterns.relationship: Decides what open areas should do; consistency repeats equivalent spatial relationships.
Supplies reference edges without specifying the intervals between elements.
Coordinates regions and spans while spacing governs repeated gaps and insets.
Defines meaningful units whose relationships repeated spacing can express.

visual_decision.reason: Three position-only transformations repeat peer entry intervals, local card insets and the gap after the final heading line while preserving all content and type styles.

sources.supports: An explicit spacing-token system based mainly on eight-pixel multiples, with exceptions; an example rather than a universal prescription.
Named spacing values, stacking and repeated spatial relationships as primary design-system guidance.
Spatial roles and keeping headings closer to the text they introduce.

patterns.title: Use Proportional Relationships
patterns.short_description: Relate selected dimensions through explicit ratios or multipliers so space and size follow content needs and remain coordinated when a reference value changes.
use_when: Equal panel shares ignore unequal reading needs.
Several type sizes are adjusted independently without a reproducible relationship.
Line spacing is unrelated to the text sizes it accompanies.
goals: Coordinate selected dimensions through explicit references.
Allocate space according to content needs.
Keep useful relationships reproducible without forcing all content into a formula.
prerequisites: Defined content roles, representative copy and an intended viewing format.
not_ideal_when: A ratio would make essential content too small or narrow.
Optical differences require adjustments to the arithmetic.
Content needs or device width call for a different arrangement.
example_user_queries: My short sidebar gets as much width as the main article.
How should I split space between instructions and facts?
The type sizes feel unrelated to each other.
Can I choose a readable base and derive the headings from it?
My smaller caption is looser than the larger paragraph.
What does a line-height multiplier actually mean?
Does using the golden ratio guarantee a better layout?
How do I know which dimensions should scale together?
Should a two-to-one layout stay that way on a phone?
The numbers are tidy but the result still looks wrong.

related_patterns.relationship: Provides tracks, regions and spans within which proportion can coordinate dimensions.
Makes a chosen priority visible; proportional rules coordinate sizes after their roles are chosen.
Repeats role-based distances; proportion can express them relative to another dimension.
Judges perceived distribution, which numerical area or size ratios cannot guarantee.

visual_decision.reason: A panel split changes with necessary instruction reflow; a type progression changes only designated font sizes; leading changes only later baselines. All photo bytes/crops and unrelated presentation remain fixed.

sources.supports: Definition of proportion as relationships between part sizes.
Primary example of coordinated geometric rules, including division, multiplication, fixed dimensions and content-dependent behavior.
Relative line-height specification and optical-size differences between typefaces.
Line height as a multiplier and contextual density considerations, rather than a universal optimum.

patterns.title: Establish Visual Rhythm
patterns.short_description: Coordinate recurring elements and intervals through deliberate repetition, variation and pauses so the composition's pace supports its content.
use_when: An isolated layout variation appears to mark a distinction the content does not have.
A meaningful section transition needs a pause within an otherwise regular run.
A short series should build toward a stated culmination.
goals: Give recurring elements a deliberate pattern.
Make variation and pauses correspond to content.
Preserve practical reading and comparison needs.
prerequisites: Content sequence, hierarchy and viewing context have been identified.
not_ideal_when: Alternation creates unnecessary searching in a comparison task.
Progression implies priorities the content does not support.
Added pauses consume space needed by practical information.
example_user_queries: One row changes sides and looks like a different category.
My layout has variety but no clear pattern.
How can a page feel varied without every section being different?
The morning and afternoon parts of my program run together.
Can I keep regular rows but add a pause at a chapter boundary?
My poster peaks on the wrong word.
How do I make three short words build toward a conclusion?
Should all of my image rows alternate sides?
When does repetition help instead of becoming monotonous?
How can I keep a visual pattern from getting in the way of reading?

related_patterns.relationship: Supplies dependable distances; rhythm concerns the larger pattern of recurrence and deliberate departures.
Gives open areas a role; pauses are one use of space within a recurring sequence.
Suggests useful destinations through direction; rhythm establishes recurrence without guaranteeing a gaze path.
Expresses priority through size; progressive rhythm applies size changes across several meaningful beats.

visual_decision.reason: The diary changes only horizontal photo/copy placement; the program moves a complete section to create a pause; the poster changes only three designated font sizes. Content, image bytes/crops and unrelated styles remain fixed.

sources.supports: Vocabulary describing rhythm through recurring elements and a sense of flow.
Identifiable design guidance distinguishing regular, alternating, progressive and flowing rhythms; not measured reader outcomes for these examples.
Repeated spacing relationships and separation between content sections.

patterns.title: Frame the Content
patterns.short_description: Define a purposeful field or boundary around content so its scope and relation to its surroundings are clear, using only the enclosure the task needs.
use_when: A boundary separates a price from details intended to explain its scope.
Essential text sits over a variable detailed photographic background.
Redundant nested boxes subdivide an already meaningful content block.
goals: Make the intended scope of a content region clear.
Provide a suitable field for text when background detail interferes.
Keep boundaries at the level the task needs.
prerequisites: The content unit and its relationship to surrounding material have been identified.
not_ideal_when: Space and alignment already express the relationship adequately.
A backing field would hide essential image detail.
Removing internal boundaries would erase useful fields or comparison structure.
example_user_queries: The price is in a box but the things it includes look separate.
Where should this border stop?
How do I show which details belong to the offer?
Text over my photograph is difficult to read in some places.
Can I add a quiet background without changing the image crop?
Does framing always mean drawing a rectangle?
Every line in my product card has a border and the block feels fragmented.
Which nested boxes should I keep?
How much content should one panel contain?
When are internal row borders actually useful?

related_patterns.relationship: Determines meaningful content units whose boundaries framing can express.
Provides open areas and internal clearance; space can sometimes define a sufficient field without an outline.
Distinguishes a subject from its surroundings; a backing field can help while enclosing a group is a separate decision.
Concentrates on enclosure as a membership cue, including correcting the apparent scope of shared information.

visual_decision.reason: Only an outline height, an opaque-field visibility value and four inner border visibility values change across three pairs. Copy, type, positions, source images/crops and presentation stay fixed.

sources.supports: Palmer 1992 common-region principle through perceptual demonstrations; abstract and publication record consulted, without claiming measured comprehension effects for the fictional layouts.
Practitioner guidance distinguishing proximity and grouping through outlined or filled regions.
Text/background contrast in a web context; used to explain the stable opaque backing field, not to claim whole-poster accessibility conformance.

patterns.title: Break the Grid Deliberately
patterns.short_description: Make a purposeful exception to a stated grid rule while keeping the surrounding structure and essential reading relationships dependable.
use_when: A template margin prevents an intended positional distinction for an opener.
An introductory image should relate to two regions rather than one column.
An expressive exception has spread unnecessarily to practical reference information.
goals: Name the rule and reason for each departure.
Keep surrounding structure legible.
Preserve grouping, practical comparisons and reading relationships.
prerequisites: A stated framework with ordinary references and allowed variants, plus a communication purpose for the exception.
not_ideal_when: The fully aligned treatment already serves the brief.
A departure obscures content or weakens meaningful grouping.
Repeated exceptions indicate that the base grid needs revision.
example_user_queries: My design feels trapped by its template even though the opener needs a different treatment.
How do I move a title into the margin without making the whole page look misaligned?
Does an image spanning two columns count as breaking the grid?
I want one image to introduce both columns of an article.
How can I keep a caption attached when its picture moves across a gutter?
The guest photo protrudes, but should the booking details protrude too?
Too many elements have their own offset and the layout has lost its references.
When should an off-grid exception become a normal template variant?
How do I preserve reading order in an expressive layout?
Would the fully aligned version be better for this task?

related_patterns.relationship: Defines ordinary references and allowed spans against which a departure can be identified.
Maintains dependable local references around a deliberate exception.
Chooses the meaningful anchor that a positional exception may reinforce.
Protects starts and continuations when meaning depends on sequence.

visual_decision.reason: Three position-only comparisons isolate a title outset, a gutter-crossing image/caption module and restoration of a booking inset while retaining an image exception. A separate diagram distinguishes an allowed span from a departure.

sources.supports: Primary design guidance combining logical repetition with expressive variation where appropriate; no measured benefit of these examples.
Flexible layout models chosen according to content needs; exact teaching-grid rules and spans are original to this article.
Preserving a programmatically determinable meaningful content sequence in digital implementations.
Digital reflow without loss of information or functionality; not a conformance claim for these fixed print artifacts.

patterns.title: Group Related Elements Through Proximity
patterns.short_description: Place elements that belong together closer to one another than to competing neighbors so distance reinforces the intended relationship.
use_when: A caption is nearly as close to another image as to the one it describes.
Titles and details form an evenly spaced stream with uncertain ownership.
Prices or other fields form a separate cluster away from their respective items.
goals: Make intended membership visible through relative distances.
Retain meaningful labels and necessary information.
Keep grouping dependable as content and available width change.
prerequisites: Accurate content, an identified viewer task and a defensible choice of which elements belong together.
not_ideal_when: A comparison table better supports cross-item inspection.
A genuinely shared note would acquire false local scope.
Reducing an internal gap would crowd the content and a different grouping cue is needed.
example_user_queries: My caption looks closer to the next picture than its own.
Which workshop does this price belong to?
Every line is equally spaced but the program feels hard to parse.
How do I show which details belong to each session?
Do related elements always need a box?
The two prices look grouped together instead of with their products.
How close should a heading be to the text it introduces?
How do I avoid making a shared note look like it applies to only one item?
Can proximity and similarity communicate different relationships?
How do I preserve groups when columns stack on mobile?

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses useful content units that proximity expresses through relative distance.
Repeats distance rules for equivalent roles after intended membership is established.
Uses shared features to connect equivalent roles across separate local groups, supporting or competing with proximity.
Concentrates on enclosure as a membership cue, including correcting the apparent scope of shared information.

visual_decision.reason: Three position-only transformations attach a caption to its image, pair detail lines with session titles, and return prices to their respective products. Image bytes, crops, wording, typography and all unrelated positions are identical.

sources.supports: Primary experimental evidence of proximity grouping in dot lattices; no numeric layout threshold or performance claim for the fictional examples.
Primary research showing that feature similarity and proximity can compete under controlled conditions.
Identifiable guidance on whitespace relationships, including headings closer to the content they introduce.
Design guidance distinguishing proximity from enclosure as grouping cues.

patterns.title: Signal Relationships Through Similarity
patterns.short_description: Give elements that share a meaningful category or role a recognizable visual feature, and avoid sharing that feature where it would imply a false relationship.
use_when: Recurring categories have inconsistent visual treatments across separated entries.
Equivalent fields use unrelated type treatments despite a comparison task.
A static fact resembles the interactive controls around it.
goals: Map repeated visual features to meaningful relationships.
Connect equivalent roles across separate local groups.
Avoid false equivalence and preserve explicit labels.
prerequisites: Accurate categories and roles, an identified viewer task and a chosen feature that remains perceptible in the intended medium.
not_ideal_when: The intended distinction is a different relationship, such as morning versus afternoon rather than activity type.
Shared appearance would imply equivalent terms or behavior that are not true.
The distinguishing feature is imperceptible at the intended reproduction size.
example_user_queries: The same event category has two different badge styles.
How can I connect recurring categories without rearranging the timetable?
Our labels look like they belong to the neighboring row instead of the same category elsewhere.
The two prices look as though they play different roles.
Can different product photos still have matching price typography?
A status message looks like another button.
Should everything with the same style do the same thing?
How do I avoid relying only on category colors?
Does consistency mean making every element identical?
When is a visual difference meaningful rather than arbitrary?

related_patterns.relationship: Uses distance to establish local membership while similarity can connect equivalent roles across those groups.
Distinguishes meaningful treatments while similarity decides where each treatment should recur.
Assigns ranks; similarity can connect peers without making them the most prominent elements.

visual_decision.reason: Three controlled comparisons align badge styles with categories, match a repeated price type role, and remove a static status from the action-like visual group. Only declared style attributes change; words, positions, image bytes/crops and presentation stay fixed.

sources.supports: Primary experimental evidence that proximity and feature similarity interact in simplified colored-shape displays; no universal cue ordering or tested benefit of these layouts.
Practitioner guidance on similarity across distributed elements and the risk of shared appearance suggesting shared functionality.
Another visual means must preserve information conveyed through color in web content; no overall conformance claim for the fictional artifacts.
Consistent button variants communicate intended functions; the example does not adopt Carbon in full.

patterns.title: Establish Visual Continuity
patterns.short_description: Make the position and direction of separated marks support the intended continuation of a path or contour, while preserving meaningful breaks.
use_when: Separated strokes should read as one contour through an intervening field.
Two connectors touch in a way that makes their intended continuations ambiguous.
A chart line bridges an unrecorded interval and implies unsupported continuity.
goals: Make intended continuations perceptually plausible.
Keep connector pairings traceable without changing their endpoints.
Preserve meaningful interruptions and distinguish observation from estimation.
mechanisms: boundary interpolation across an occluding field
prerequisites: Correct connections or data, a stated reason for continuity and a distinction between conceptual and physically constrained routes.
not_ideal_when: Separate strokes are deliberately independent accents.
A bend represents an actual obstacle, boundary or abrupt event.
Connecting marks would imply a relationship or measurement that is not supported.
example_user_queries: The rule looks broken when it passes behind the title panel.
The two line fragments have the same angle but do not feel like one line.
Which branch am I supposed to follow at this connector crossing?
My curves touch and seem to connect to the wrong labels.
Can I reroute these lines without moving their endpoints?
Does every connection need to be drawn without a gap?
The report draws a trend through a week we did not record.
Should missing data be connected, left open or shown as zero?
Does a continuous line guarantee the reader will follow it?
How do I keep decorative rules from looking like part of the chart?

related_patterns.relationship: Connects directional cues to useful destinations; continuity determines which marks appear to belong to the same contour.
Establishes spatial references; continuity also concerns direction across gaps, curves and crossings.
Connects elements by shared appearance; continuity adds the positional and directional relation between segments.
Concerns a larger form inferred from visible evidence; continuous contours need not imply a closed whole.

visual_decision.reason: Three controlled comparisons align a diagonal across an opaque title field, clarify connector continuations while retaining endpoints, and remove a missing-data bridge without altering observations. Only declared line attributes change; content, styling, image data/crops and presentation remain fixed.

sources.supports: Primary contour-integration experiments showing alignment effects in detecting paths among oriented distractors; no measured reading or fixation benefit for these designs.
Original theory of boundary interpolation and partial occlusion; application to the poster is editorial interpretation.
Official documentation distinguishing interpolation, gaps and zero as different missing-value treatments; no universal recommendation for all datasets.

patterns.title: Separate Figure from Ground
patterns.short_description: Give the content that must read as a distinct object or layer a dependable boundary against its surroundings, using a ground that supports that distinction.
use_when: Light lettering competes with bright detail in a photographic ground.
A dark product contour merges with a similarly dark backdrop.
A dialog and the underlying page have insufficient visual distinction as layers.
goals: Make necessary objects, words and layers distinguishable from their surroundings.
Choose a ground treatment that preserves useful context.
Distinguish perceptual separation from prominence, text contrast and implemented modal behavior.
prerequisites: A stated figure and purpose, appropriate imagery, and a decision about which contextual details must remain available.
not_ideal_when: Ambiguity or a low-key image is an intentional expressive aim and necessary information remains accessible.
A strong shade or surface hides context essential to understanding the subject.
Users need to consult or interact with the surrounding page and a modal layer is inappropriate.
example_user_queries: The words disappear where they cross bright parts of the photograph.
The photo is mostly dark but some of the type is still hard to read.
My product disappears into its backdrop.
How can I show the handle shape without drawing an outline around it?
Can I change just the background while keeping the same product photograph?
The dialog looks like another section of the page.
Which layer of this screen is the current task?
Does every foreground object need a shadow?
Will dimming the background make a dialog function accessibly?
When is an ambiguous figure and background relationship appropriate?

related_patterns.relationship: Gives differences meaningful roles, including between peers; figure-ground concerns a chosen object relative to its surrounding field.
Defines fields and boundaries; a backing surface can help separate content, while an outline alone may not reduce background interference.
Allocates open areas that can clarify an outline without changing colors or adding surfaces.
Chooses a leading role; supporting figures can remain distinct without competing to lead.

visual_decision.reason: Three controlled comparisons shade a photographic ground beneath fixed light lettering, change only the backdrop of an identical transparent product file, and dim a page beneath an unchanged opaque dialog. Their different ground interventions isolate legibility, contour inspection and layer separation.

sources.supports: Expert account by Peterson and Salvagio of figure-ground perception, including border assignment and the ground appearing to continue behind a figure.
Primary experiment showing that symmetry and recognition-related cues both influence figure-ground reports; no validation of the fictional designs.
Sufficient local text/background luminance contrast and background-image failures; the limited contrast bound is not a whole-artifact conformance claim.
Modal-dialog background inertness and focus management are distinct from the customary visual dimming.

patterns.title: Use Implied Forms
patterns.short_description: Leave parts of a visual form undrawn or hidden while retaining enough contour and identifying features for the intended whole to remain recognizable.
use_when: A complete outline adds more drawn boundary than the brief needs.
A graphic motif crosses an object even though the hidden contour can be inferred.
An abstract icon lacks the feature that identifies its intended object.
goals: Preserve enough visible evidence to support the intended whole.
Use omission or occlusion without hiding essential meaning.
Restore identifying features when abstraction weakens recognition.
prerequisites: A chosen form and purpose, sufficient identifying evidence, and explicit labels or facts where recognition alone is insufficient.
not_ideal_when: The boundary must specify an exact area or functional region.
An unfamiliar or small symbol cannot be recognized reliably from the remaining fragments.
Omission hides content, terms or action meaning rather than merely visual contour.
example_user_queries: Can I suggest a rectangle without drawing the entire box?
The border feels heavier than the information needs.
The decorative circle runs across the product surface.
Can the circle disappear behind the object and still read as a whole?
How much of this outline can I leave out?
The icon is minimal but nobody knows what it represents.
Which feature should I add back to make this shape recognizable?
Is a broken contour always better than a complete one?
Does recognizing the icon mean its action is clear?
When should I keep a full boundary instead of implying it?

related_patterns.relationship: Connects contour segments through direction and position; implied forms concern the larger whole they suggest.
Distinguishes the foreground object and the ground, supporting a plausible interpretation of partly occluded forms.
Chooses a field’s scope and purpose; partial contour is one way of expressing the chosen field.
Evaluates contributions to communication; necessary identifying features must be retained or restored.

visual_decision.reason: Three controlled transformations replace continuous edges with fixed corners, switch the same circle behind a fixed product, and restore a folded-corner cue to an incomplete file icon. All words, photographs, crops, geometry unrelated to the intervention, type and presentation remain fixed.

sources.supports: Original theory of visual interpolation addressing partial occlusion and illusory figures; no guarantee that every incomplete design is recognized.
Primary experiments relating judged boundary clarity to specified versus total edge length in controlled illusory-figure displays; no universal deletion percentage for design.
Practitioner guidance on incomplete forms, preserving sufficient evidence, testing icon understanding and retaining clear labels.

patterns.title: Group Elements Within Shared Boundaries
patterns.short_description: Enclose elements that belong to the same meaningful unit, keeping unrelated elements outside so the visible region expresses the intended membership.
use_when: Details distributed across a layout need to read as one complete record.
A boundary makes shared terms look specific to one offer.
Existing containers group attributes when the reader needs complete options.
goals: Make enclosure express intended membership.
Preserve shared conditions outside offer-specific regions.
Choose grouping units appropriate to the reader’s task.
mechanisms: scope expressed through inclusion and exclusion
prerequisites: Meaningful content units and a clear task; sufficient clearance between text and enclosing edge.
not_ideal_when: Spacing and typography already communicate the intended units reliably.
Categories overlap in ways exclusive containers would misrepresent.
Attribute-by-attribute comparison is more useful than grouping complete options.
example_user_queries: Which details should share one box?
People read the room and price as a separate list.
Can a boundary connect details across two columns?
This delivery note applies to both products but looks attached to one.
Should shared conditions sit inside or outside these offer cards?
Do these boxes group the product or its attributes?
Should I use rows or cards for this comparison?
Do I need a box if spacing already shows the groups?
How do I avoid putting every sentence in a separate container?
Does a visible form outline make its fields semantically related?

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses meaningful content units; shared regions make their membership visible.
Uses relative distance rather than enclosure to express membership; the cues should agree.
Connects categories or roles through repeated appearance, including across separate regions.
Establishes useful scope and fields through margins, surfaces and boundaries; shared regions concentrate on implied membership.

visual_decision.reason: Three boundary-only transformations add complete session regions, release shared delivery terms from one offer, and change the grouping axis from attributes to complete offers. Copy, positions, typography, image bytes/crops, paper and lighting stay fixed.

sources.supports: Original common-region demonstrations show enclosure influences perceived grouping and can overcome proximity or similarity; no universal claim about cards or tested benefit for these artifacts.
Identifiable guidance distinguishes proximity and shared-region grouping through outlines and background fields.
Form grouping should be expressed visually and programmatically; fieldsets and legends associate related controls.

patterns.title: Match Typeface to Context
patterns.short_description: Choose a typeface and its appropriate cut for the reader’s task, intended voice, required characters, and actual viewing and production conditions.
use_when: A display-oriented cut has been carried into sustained small text.
A headline’s visual voice does not serve the specific communication brief.
Required code characters or language details are poorly distinguished or unsupported.
goals: Select letterforms and optical cuts appropriate to reading conditions.
Support an intended voice without stereotyping type categories.
Inspect the exact required characters and font delivery conditions.
prerequisites: A defined reader task, actual copy, intended medium and viewing conditions, and usable licensed font files.
not_ideal_when: The real failure is missing content, contrast, scale, line length or spacing.
An established identity already supports the brief and a change would be arbitrary.
A code-generation or content-system change can remove ambiguity more directly.
example_user_queries: The font looks elegant in the mockup but fragile in the small printed text.
Can I keep the same family and use a different cut for body copy?
The headline does not feel like the event we are inviting people to.
How do I choose between an expressive face and our usual brand font?
People cannot tell capital I from lowercase l in this reference.
The zero and letter O look too similar on our collection slips.
Does a monospace font always make a code readable?
Why do two fonts at the same size look different?
How should I check accents and required symbols before choosing a font?
Should I change the font or fix the line spacing first?

related_patterns.relationship: Defines the reader’s tasks, knowledge and viewing conditions that inform type selection.
Selects structure and medium for the communication; typeface choice operates within that decision.
Changes relative size to express priority; typeface selection changes letterform design for contextual fitness.
Considers how multiple suitable faces work together and retain stable roles across the design.

visual_decision.reason: Three font-selection-only transformations move body copy between optical cuts, change a headline voice for an event brief, and differentiate reference-code characters. Embedded licensed font instances prevent fallback. Nominal sizes, weights, positions, line breaks, copy, colors, image bytes/crops and presentation stay fixed. Natural font metrics differ.

sources.supports: The family designer explains optical-size changes to spacing, proportions and details, and emphasizes viewing distance/output rather than prescriptive size labels.
Identifiable type-design guidance distinguishes display expression and small-text requirements without presenting a universal category rule.
The designers document a display typeface with softness and unconventional form features; the supper interpretation remains editorial.
The font creator explains differentiated character forms and its monospaced family; this does not establish measured transcription benefits for the example.
Clear readable type must be combined with adaptable setting; no single font is fully accessible to all users.

patterns.title: Pair Complementary Typefaces
patterns.short_description: Give selected typefaces distinct, compatible roles and apply those roles consistently so the combination supports one communication purpose.
use_when: Two expressive faces compete without a meaningful division of labor.
A second family contributes little to the role or voice requested by the brief.
The same two faces swap jobs between equivalent entries.
goals: Make each selected typeface contribute a useful role.
Coordinate contrast and coherence rather than maximizing difference.
Apply the relationship consistently across repeated content.
mechanisms: stable mapping of visual treatments to roles
prerequisites: A clear communication purpose, actual copy and intended roles; readable individual faces, licensed files and suitable setting.
not_ideal_when: One capable family already supplies the required range.
Typeface variation deliberately identifies contributors or categories rather than content roles.
The underlying failure is content, size, spacing, line length or accessibility rather than interaction between faces.
example_user_queries: The heading and supporting text both feel like they are trying to lead.
These fonts look good individually but feel unrelated together.
Does my second font actually contribute anything?
Two sans serif fonts look almost the same on this page.
How can I get a clearer title voice without changing the layout?
Should I choose coordinated serif and sans families?
Our two fonts keep swapping jobs between entries.
Which font should handle descriptions and practical information?
Do I really need another typeface for captions and prices?
Can I use one family instead of a font pair?

related_patterns.relationship: Evaluates each face for its task; pairing evaluates how selected faces interact.
Gives visible differences useful jobs; typeface pairing is a specific relational application.
Establishes meaningful ranks, while typeface changes can also distinguish equal-status voices.
Maps repeated treatments to intended roles, including consistent assignments within a two-face system.

visual_decision.reason: Three controlled photographic transformations replace a competing script supporting voice, give a near-similar pair a distinct title role, and stabilize the same two faces across repeated entries. Only declared font-family assignments change; exact copy, nominal sizes, requested weights, baselines, anchors, line breaks, colors, image bytes/crops and presentation remain fixed. Natural font metrics differ.

sources.supports: Identifiable pairing guidance discusses contrast, similarity, coordinated families and testing combinations in context rather than a universal pairing formula.
A documented identity assigns expressive work to Plex Mono and supporting information to Plex Sans; its role system is an example rather than a universal prescription.
The font project identifies Source Serif as a companion to Source Sans; this design intention does not guarantee every chosen setting.

patterns.title: Establish a Type Scale
patterns.short_description: Choose a limited set of type sizes, assign them to recurring text roles, and adapt the relationships to the medium while preserving readable supporting text.
use_when: Equivalent text roles have accumulated unrelated size variations.
Page and section levels are nearly equal despite a meaningful hierarchy.
A display-heavy role set needs adapting without shrinking supporting text.
goals: Assign repeated roles to a manageable set of sizes.
Separate meaningful text levels while preserving readable detail.
Adapt the role values to medium and task rather than enforcing a universal ratio.
prerequisites: Meaningful content roles, a suitable font and readable supporting size for the medium and viewing conditions.
not_ideal_when: A one-off expressive composition needs justified optical exceptions.
The content hierarchy has not yet been decided.
The primary problem is unsuitable letterforms, line length, spacing or missing information.
example_user_queries: Our programme has a slightly different font size for every text box.
Why do equivalent activity names look like different levels?
How many type sizes does this page actually need?
The page title and section headings look almost equal.
Can we reuse a small size set across our printed materials?
Does a type scale need to follow one mathematical ratio?
Our booking screen feels like a promotional poster.
How can we reduce large headings without making the body smaller?
Do labels and body text need different sizes?
Should one long title be shrunk or should the component wrap?

related_patterns.relationship: Decides meaningful ranks; the scale supplies recurring size relationships to express them.
Makes an intended priority visible; a type scale coordinates recurring text roles across a system.
Selects letterforms and optical cuts; changing the font requires reassessing the numerical scale.
Coordinates repeated intervals around text; production must coordinate spacing with size even though it is held fixed in these comparisons.

visual_decision.reason: Three strict size-only comparisons consolidate eight sizes into four repeated print roles, separate nearly equal heading levels using the same scale, and adapt upper phone roles without shrinking body or metadata. Exact copy, font file, optical design, weights, anchors, baselines, line breaks, images/crops, colors and presentation remain fixed.

sources.supports: A documented scale coordinates sizes and line heights, supports reusable styles, and changes selected larger roles across screen ranges while retaining some smaller steps.
Documented productive/expressive type sets and consistency within tasks/regions support contextual scale choices rather than one immutable ladder.
Choosing scale values does not establish implemented text enlargement without loss of content or function; static illustrations do not demonstrate resizing compliance.

patterns.title: Control Line Length
patterns.short_description: Set the width available to prose so lines support the reading task, allowing natural reflow while preserving readable type and accommodating the surrounding layout.
use_when: Prose inherits an expansive page width despite being read continuously.
A narrow grid span fragments ordinary sentences into very short lines.
A prose summary needs a different width from the table or other wide content beside it.
goals: Select a reading measure appropriate to the text and task.
Preserve readable typography while changing horizontal allocation.
Allow prose to reflow without restricting unrelated functional content.
mechanisms: horizontal distance between line end and next start
text measure independent of page width
prerequisites: Suitable font and reading size, actual language/copy, space for the resulting reflow and a defined reading task.
not_ideal_when: A label, poem, brief caption or constrained panel legitimately requires a different measure.
The real problem is unclear content, inappropriate type size or insufficient leading.
A rigid preferred character count would cause clipping or horizontal scrolling under text enlargement.
example_user_queries: Our landscape guide has very long lines of prose.
Should the paragraph really fill the whole page?
This care note wraps every few words.
Can I widen the column without making the type smaller?
How many characters per line should I aim for?
Does shorter text measure always mean faster reading?
The report table needs more width than its introduction.
Can the prose have its own maximum width?
Should I add manual line breaks or change the text box?
What happens to a reading width when someone enlarges text?

related_patterns.relationship: Chooses letterforms whose widths affect the measure needed for a given amount of text.
Supplies the spatial framework; prose can use a selected span independently of wider functional content.
Changes the baseline interval; consider it alongside how much text each line carries.
Refines local breaks and phrasing within a given measure without changing reading width.

visual_decision.reason: Three exact-font comparisons narrow expansive guide prose, widen fragmented care instructions and cap a summary independently of its table. Only the declared measure and necessary word wrapping change. All words, font/size/weight, leading, left edge, first baseline, image bytes/crops and presentation remain fixed. patterns.title: Adjust Letter Spacing

patterns.title: Limit the Palette
